content: An antigen, derived from the term antibody-generating, is a molecule capable of eliciting an immune response. Initially, the term was based on the idea that antigens stimulate the production of antibodies. However, it is now understood that the immune system is not solely reliant on antibodies. The modern definition of an antigen includes any substance that can be recognized by the adaptive immune system. Antigens are typically proteins or polysaccharides and can include structural components of microorganisms such as bacterial coats, capsules, cell walls, flagella, fimbriae, and toxins. Lipids and nucleic acids are only antigenic when they are associated with proteins or polysaccharides. Non-microbial antigens, which originate from external sources, include substances like pollen, egg white, and proteins found in transplanted tissues, organs, or transfused blood cells. A tolerogen is a specific type of antigen that induces immune tolerance, meaning it does not provoke an immune response due to its molecular structure. However, if its molecular structure changes, a tolerogen can become an immunogen, which does stimulate an immune response. An allergen, on the other hand, is a type of antigen that triggers an allergic reaction. Antigens are presented to the immune system by cells using histocompatibility molecules. The type of antigen and the histocompatibility molecule involved determine which immune cells are activated. Origin of Antigens Antigens can be categorized based on their origin: Exogenous Antigens Exogenous antigens are those that enter the body from external sources, such as through inhalation, ingestion, or injection. These antigens are internalized by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) via endocytosis or phagocytosis and are subsequently broken down into smaller fragments. The APCs then present these fragments to CD4+ T helper cells using class II histocompatibility molecules on their surface. T cells that are specific to the peptide-MHC complex become activated and release cytokines. These cytokines, in turn, activate other immune cells, including cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), B cells that secrete antibodies, macrophages, and other immune components. Endogenous Antigens Endogenous antigens are generated within a cell, either as a result of normal cellular processes or due to infections caused by viruses or intracellular bacteria. These antigens are processed into fragments and presented on the cell surface in association with MHC class I molecules. If cytotoxic CD8+ T cells recognize these antigen-MHC complexes, they release toxins that induce lysis or apoptosis of the infected cell. To prevent cytotoxic T cells from attacking normal cells presenting self-proteins, self-reactive T cells are eliminated during a process called negative selection, which occurs during immune tolerance development. Autoantigens Autoantigens are typically normal proteins or protein complexes (and occasionally DNA or RNA) that are mistakenly targeted by the immune system in individuals with autoimmune diseases. Under normal circumstances, these antigens should not provoke an immune response. However, due to genetic predispositions and environmental factors, the immune system loses tolerance to these self-antigens, leading to autoimmune conditions. Tumor Antigens Tumor antigens, also referred to as neoantigens, are antigens presented on the surface of tumor cells by MHC class I or II molecules. Tumor-specific antigens (TSAs) are exclusively expressed by tumor cells and arise from tumor-specific mutations. In contrast, tumor-associated antigens (TAAs) are expressed by both tumor cells and normal cells. Cytotoxic T lymphocytes that recognize these antigens may destroy tumor cells before they proliferate or metastasize. Tumor antigens can also exist on the tumor cell surface, such as mutated receptors, which can be recognized by B cells. Native Antigens A native antigen is an antigen that has not yet been processed into smaller fragments by an antigen-presenting cell (APC). T cells cannot directly bind to native antigens; they require the antigen to be processed and presented by APCs. In contrast, B cells can recognize and be activated by native antigens without prior processing.
